title: Ezra 8:31–36
context: The company leaves the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month and reaches Jerusalem safely, for, as Ezra says, “The hand of our God was on us” (8:31). After three days, the silver, gold, and vessels are weighed and recorded in the house of God, and the returned exiles offer burnt offerings and sin offerings “for all Israel” (8:35), including twelve bulls and twelve male goats, as at the dedication of the temple, when twelve goats were offered for all Israel (6:17). The king’s commissions are delivered to the regional officials, who support the people and God’s house (8:36). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God keeps his people on the way, faithful stewardship is honored, and worship for all Israel is renewed.

verses.text: Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and the bandits by the way.
verses.arminianNotes: They leave the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, and Ezra says, “The hand of our God was on us,” for God delivered them from enemies and bandits. Arminian readers see God’s protection answering their prayer and honoring their trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s hand guarding his people on the way, as Ezra had confessed before the king (8:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a testimony to God’s faithful protection, and both treat the hand of God as common ground rather than a point of dispute.

verses.text: We came to Jerusalem, and stayed there three days.
verses.arminianNotes: They come to Jerusalem and rest three days. Arminian readers note the completion of a long and dangerous journey. The pause allows the travelers to recover before taking up the next responsibilities.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the safe arrival as the fulfillment of God’s protection. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a simple record of arrival and rest, and both see in it God’s faithfulness to the travelers who trusted him.

verses.text: On the fourth day the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed in the house of our God into the hand of Meremoth the son of Uriah the priest; and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas; and with them were Jozabad the son of Jeshua, and Noadiah the son of Binnui, the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes: On the fourth day the silver, gold, and vessels are weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest and others in the house of God. Arminian readers note the careful handover, with priests and Levites present. Faithful stewardship continues to the end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the completion of the accountability set up in 8:24–29. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing integrity in handling sacred gifts and see in it a model for the faithful management of what belongs to God.

verses.text: Everything was counted and weighed; and all the weight was written at that time.
verses.arminianNotes: Everything is counted and weighed, and the total is recorded. Arminian readers note that nothing is lost or left unaccounted for. The written record protects the reputation of those who carried the offering and honors the givers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the thoroughness of the accounting as fitting for gifts dedicated to God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming transparency and faithfulness, and both see in it God’s protection of the offering on the way.

verses.text: The children of the captivity, who had come out of exile, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats for a sin offering. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The returned exiles offer burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve goats for a sin offering. Arminian readers note that the returnees respond to God’s faithfulness with worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see grateful worship and note that the offerings are made “for all Israel,” as at the temple’s dedication (6:17). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as thanksgiving and atonement for the whole people, and neither builds a further doctrine on the numbers.

verses.text: They delivered the king’s commissions to the king’s local governors and to the governors beyond the River. So they supported the people and God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: They deliver the king’s commissions to the governors beyond the River, who support the people and God’s house. Arminian readers note that the king’s decree is carried out, and that the officials’ support follows from it. The mission ends in success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s provision completed through the cooperation of the king’s officials. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the conclusion of Ezra’s journey and see in it the faithful working of God’s good hand from beginning to end.
